Title: Source 1: Should Community Service Be a Requirement?
Author: by Diana Redly
Content: High schools across the country are requiring that their students complete community service `text(hours)`. This has been a topic of debate, because some believe that volunteering shouldn't be something that students are forced to do. Volunteering, after all, should be voluntary, shouldn't it?

Studies have shown that students who participate in community service tend to get better grades. This may be due to learning opportunities presented by service projects, or a heightened sense of belonging. Studies have also shown that individuals who volunteer tend to be healthier and happier than those who don't.

Volunteering also strengthens college applications. In a survey of college admissions officers, `text(84 percent)` said that “a student's community service has a positive impact on acceptance to our higher education institution.” Colleges seek students who understand the value of helping others and have good time management skills. Being involved in community service outside of school `text(hours)` while balancing schoolwork shows a high level of responsibility.

Participating in community service also builds career-readiness skills like collaboration, communication, and leadership. If students learn how to work well with others while volunteering in high school, they will be better prepared for the professional world.

However, there are many high school students who are already part of the workforce. Afterschool jobs can teach students the same skills that unpaid volunteer opportunities do. Students who hold jobs might find it challenging to also complete the number of volunteer `text(hours)` required by the school. This can make community service feel like a burden rather than an enjoyable and meaningful experience.

While requiring students to participate in community service may create a sense of civic responsibility, students do not necessarily carry this with them after graduation. `text(One)` study by the National Center for Education Statistics reported that after high school, young adults were less active as community service members. In fact, `text(eight years)` after graduation, volunteerism declined by `text(25 percent)`. When community service is no longer mandatory, young people may lose motivation to spend their limited free time volunteering.

Yet, the communities themselves greatly benefit from youth volunteerism. For example, teens across Florida develop their own service projects as a component of their International Baccalaureate program. At `text(one)` school in South Florida, teachers encourage students to be creative with their projects and choose something that they are passionate about. `text(One)` group of high school students developed a program to give free music lessons to children in the community. These children were eager to work with the students and gained an appreciation for the arts. Another student group organized community walks to raise money for local charities. These walks will continue to raise more and more money as incoming students offer new ideas.
